answer.conclusion:
The preferred reading separates confirmation from request-triggered demonstration. The request qualification appears after the conjunction and immediately before demonstration: Product Providers should confirm without awaiting a request and, upon request, demonstrate to the SFC’s satisfaction. Both verbs share all three objects: management and operational soundness of the tokenisation arrangement, record keeping of ownership, and integrity of the smart contracts. Demonstration is not confined to smart-contract integrity. The satisfaction standard attaches most directly to demonstration, although a shared-standard reading remains supported.

The explanatory footnote identifies the SFC as recipient of both acts and specifies minimum substantive content: compliance with the incorporated operational requirements and a high-confidence showing that smart contracts are not subject to contract vulnerabilities or security flaws. High confidence most naturally qualifies the security proposition, although attachment to the combined showing is possible. It describes confidence in the absence of vulnerabilities or flaws, not a restriction to particularly severe flaws. The supplied wording gives no numerical confidence threshold, guarantee against future flaws or replacement for the SFC-satisfaction standard.

The strongest reconciliation treats the footnote as elaborating substance while retaining the main sentence’s express request condition. Without an SFC request, confirmation therefore remains expected, but the specified demonstration requirement is not activated on that reading. The footnote’s unqualified repetition of both verbs nevertheless supports a genuine rival under which demonstration is independently expected. A reading that makes both verbs request-dependent is weaker but cannot be conclusively excluded. None of these readings suspends the underlying substantive responsibilities.

The neighbouring provisions concern procurement rather than simply the Provider’s own confirmation and demonstration. One expressly requires, upon SFC request, third-party audit or verification concerning the same operational, ownership-record and smart-contract matters. Audit and verification are textual alternatives, not an express requirement to obtain both; this sentence does not repeat the SFC-satisfaction standard. The other expressly calls, upon request, for a satisfactory legal opinion supporting the application. Its application-supporting purpose is clear, but the precise legal questions and evaluator of satisfaction are unspecified. Neither form of procurement expressly substitutes for the other or for confirmation and requested demonstration. The actual scope of the SFC communication determines which expectations it activates.

Without the relevant requests, these procurement expectations are not activated by their own wording. That is not a general exemption from assessment or assurance: the supplied technical appendix conditionally contemplates technology audits, smart-contract audits and justified reliance on third-party work. Its intermediary-facing considerations inform Providers where applicable; they do not establish a universal mandatory audit procedure or safe harbour. Providers retain ultimate responsibility despite outsourcing. Proper ownership records, operational compatibility, cybersecurity and other risk measures, recovery arrangements, robust business continuity and additional proper controls for public-permissionless networks remain substantive expectations.

These are regulatory expectations expressed using ‘should’, not proof of a freestanding statutory liability rule. Confirmation, outsourcing, obtaining an assurance report or submitting an opinion does not establish the underlying outcomes or SFC satisfaction. The Handbook separately distinguishes regulatory and evidential consequences from automatic liability for non-compliance, and authorisation does not itself establish compliance with all applicable requirements.

5 Product Providers should confirm and demonstrate to the SFC that, at a minimum, they comply with the requirements as set out in paragraphs 10 to 13 above and the smart contracts are not subject to any contract vulnerabilities or security flaws with a high level of confidence.

Product Providers should, upon SFC’s request, obtain third party audit or verification on the management and operational soundness of the tokenisation arrangement, record keeping of ownership and integrity of the smart contracts.
Product Providers should, upon SFC’s request, obtain satisfactory legal opinion to support its application.

Product Providers should remain and be ultimately responsible for the management and operational soundness of the tokenisation arrangement adopted and record keeping of ownership, regardless of any outsourcing arrangement1.

Product Providers should ensure that proper records of token holders’ ownership interests in the product are maintained and the tokenisation arrangement is operationally compatible with service providers involved2.

Product Providers should have appropriate measures in place to manage and mitigate cybersecurity risks3, data privacy, system outages and recovery, and maintain a comprehensive and robust business continuity plan.
Product Providers should not use public-permissionless blockchain networks without additional and proper controls (eg, Product Providers to impose additional control by using a permissioned token)4.

1 Given that these tokenised products are offered to the public in Hong Kong and the importance of maintaining proper records to reflect investors’ ownership, the Product Provider should remain fully responsible, despite any outsourcing arrangement such as those envisaged under 6.8 of the Code on Unit Trusts and Mutual Funds. For factors of consideration, please also refer to Part A of the Appendix to the Tokenised Securities Circular, where applicable, when formulating the tokenisation arrangement.

By adopting a see-through approach, the SFC is of the view that it is appropriate to allow primary dealing of tokenised SFC-authorised investment products, as long as the underlying product can meet all the applicable product authorisation requirements and the additional safeguards to address the new risks associated with the tokenisation arrangement (as set out in paragraphs 10-19 below).

Product providers of tokenised SFC-authorised investment products (Product Providers) should ensure that the underlying products should meet the applicable requirements in the relevant rules and regulations, and product codes (including eligibility of Product Providers, product structure, investment and operational requirements, disclosure and ongoing compliance obligations).

Additional requirements set out below, as well as the relevant requirements in the Circular on intermediaries engaging in tokenised securities-related activities issued by the SFC (Tokenised Securities Circular), should also be satisfied.

Chapter 1: Preliminary
      Introduction to the Handbook

1.1   The Handbook is made under section 399 of the SFO and establishes codes or
      guidelines for the authorization of products covered by the Handbook and their offering
      documents and advertisements. These guidelines are not intended to be exhaustive.

1.2   Section I of the Handbook sets out the high-level principles and requirements that are
      intended to apply to all products. More detailed product-specific requirements applicable
      to specific types of products are contained in the applicable product code.

1.3   The Handbook provides general guidelines for authorization of products specifically
      stated in the applicable product codes. The Commission will have regard to both the
      spirit as well as the letter of the General Principles set out in Chapter 3 of this
      Overarching Principles Section in considering products authorization applications and
      whether products should remain authorized.

1.4   All products, their Product Providers and the Specified Entities are expected to comply
      with all applicable principles and requirements set out in Section I of the Handbook in
      addition to the detailed product-specific requirements applicable to specific types of
      products that are contained in the applicable product code.

1.5   The Handbook does not have the force of law and shall not be interpreted in a way that
      will override the provision of any law.
